newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela's Caldera to address Colombia relations.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela's Caldera to address Colombia relations.

text.p: Venezuela's President Rafael Caldera will make a nationwide address on Wednesday about relations with Colombia after two Venezuelan soldiers were injured in a cross-border attack.
"This evening there will be a nationwide broadcast and the subject is Colombia," a presidential press spokesman said. The broadcast was scheduled for 8 p.m local time (Midnight GMT).

Earlier five soldiers on patrol were ambushed by presumed Colombian guerrillas in the Paez district of Apure state, two miles (3 km) from the border. Two paratroopers were seriously wounded in an hour-long gunbattle that ensued, Defence Minister Tito Rincon Bravo said.

"(The attack) was immediately repelled by the soldiers and the Air Force was alerted, which sent two Bronco planes and a helicopter to monitor the area," Rincon said. He said the two wounded soldiers were under observation but out of danger.

He could not confirm a report by local Union Radio that the attack was carried out by a column of between 25 and 30 rebels of Colombia's leftist National Liberation Army (ELN). But it was the most serious attack along the frontier since two soldiers were killed by ELN rebels in April.

The presidential palace spokesman said Caldera would speak about the recent attacks and clarify his position on overtures made by Colombian guerrilla groups wanting to start a dialogue with the Venezuelan government.

Colombia's President Ernesto Samper, who recently launched a new peace process to try to end a three-decade-old guerrilla uprising, phoned Caldera on Monday to ask him not to start talks with the ELN and the larger Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).
Venezuelan government officials have said Caracas would talk to the Marxist groups only with Bogota's consent.
Venezuela frequently criticises Colombia for inadequate security along the 1,400 mile (2,200 km) border where smuggling, kidnapping and armed skirmishes have become increasingly frequent.
